notes.body:
There is a distinction at the heart of every genuine spiritual tradition, and al-Ghazali names it plainly here. Some knowledge can be set down in ink — it describes obligations, maps the outward road, clarifies what is required. But there is another kind that **writing cannot carry**: the inner reality, الباطن, which does not explain but transforms, and transforms only through direct encounter, teacher to student, when the student is ready to receive.

The authority that forbids writing is not a human institution — it is the nature of the knowledge itself. To commit these inner realities to paper risks two things:

- The unprepared reader mistakes the description for the thing itself, and stops traveling
- The words, stripped of their living context, become a cage rather than a door

This is why the passage turns immediately to the story of خضر and Musa — even a prophet was told not to ask until his teacher chose the moment to speak.

فَلاَ تَسْئَلْنِي عَنْ شَيْءٍ حَتَّى أُحْدِثَ لَكَ مِنْهُ ذِكْرًا
"Do not question me about anything until I myself bring it up to you and explain it."
Al-Kahf 18:70

The teacher **protects**. Knowledge given before its time does not illuminate; it confuses, and sometimes destroys. The seeker's capacity must grow to meet the knowledge, not the other way around. Act upon what you already know, and through that acting, what you do not yet know will be unveiled. The road itself is the teacher — and it only speaks to those already walking it.
notes.anchor: some are such that to write their answers is not permitted
notes.quote: some are such that to write their answers is not permitted
etymology: الباطن (the inner, the hidden): from the root ب-ط-ن, meaning the belly or interior of a thing. Just as the belly holds nourishment before the body is ready to use it, الباطن is the inward face of reality — the living truth concealed beneath the outward form, waiting until the soul matures enough to receive it without harm.

خضر (the Evergreen One): from the root خ-ض-ر, meaning to be green, fresh, and perpetually verdant. الخضر — the teacher who never withers — carries his wisdom in his very name: living knowledge that cannot be pressed between the pages of a book, always renewed, always timed to the readiness of the one who stands before him.

notes.body:
The tongue of the heart (لسان القلب) is not a quiet prayer or an inward whisper. It is the soul's own readiness — the genuine need that forms inside a seeker only after he has walked far enough along the road to receive what he is reaching for.

When the teacher says "ask me only through the tongue of the heart," he is drawing a line between two kinds of questioning. A verbal question can arrive from anywhere — curiosity, impatience, the wish to seem eager. The heart's question cannot be manufactured; it only takes shape once the soul has prepared itself through obedience, contentment, and sincerity (إِخْلَاص).

So how does a student actually use it? Not by sitting still and thinking harder. The three Quranic verses the teacher quotes all give the same method: wait with patience, do not hasten, travel through the earth and see. The student works, endures, stays within the Shariah, and as that practice deepens him, what he needs to know surfaces on its own.

The difference from asking in words is a difference of **source**. A word-question comes from the mind; it can arrive before the student is ready, it can be driven by رِيَاء, and it pulls the teacher away from the right moment. The heart-question arises from the soul's actual condition. Khidr's instruction — "do not question me about anything until I myself bring it up" — is exactly this: right knowledge comes at the right moment, and forcing it with words breaks the timing.

At its root, the tongue of the heart is tawakkul (تَوَكُّل) applied to learning — the trust that what Allah has written for you will reach you, and that what He has not written will not come no matter how urgently you ask.
notes.anchor: do not ask me about what is difficult for you except through the tong…
notes.quote: do not ask me about what is difficult for you except through the tongue of the heart
etymology: لسان (tongue): from the root ل-س-ن, linked to the organ of speech and to language itself. The root carries a sense of fluency and moisture — the tongue as what gives inner meaning an outward shape. When the teacher speaks of the لسان القلب, he is saying: let the heart speak with its own native voice, not borrowed words.

قلب (heart): from ق-ل-ب, meaning to flip or turn something over. The heart is named for its constant turning — between states of fear and hope, contraction and openness. It is never fixed, which is why its language is a live orientation rather than a fixed question.

تَوَكُّل (reliance on Allah): from و-ك-ل, to delegate or entrust. The تَفَعُّل pattern makes the act reflexive and intensive — you actively hand yourself over. Not passive resignation, but the deliberate placing of your affairs in Allah's hands.

إِخْلَاص (sincerity): from خ-ل-ص, to be freed from mixture, to be refined. Like purifying metal by removing alloy. إِخْلَاص is the state of an act with no foreign motive remaining — intention directed to Allah alone, unmixed.

رِيَاء (ostentation): from ر-أ-ي, to see. رِيَاء is the act of making yourself seen — performing for an audience. The root exposes the disease: an action infected by the gaze of others, when it should exist only before Allah.
